old: This word is built from a piece meaning 'around, about' attached to something you'd lay down against a fortress.
Strip away the prefix meaning 'around' and you're left with the word for a prolonged military blockade.
It shares its core with 'siege' — just wrapped in the idea of being encircled.
clues: This verb of warfare was built by fastening an old prefix meaning 'around, about' onto an existing military word, so the action literally encircles its target.
It means to surround a city or fortress with an army to force surrender. That is more than simply attacking or encircling it, since supplies are cut off until defenders give in.
Beyond armies, a celebrity can be ___ by reporters or a help desk ___ with requests. Its closest relative is the noun for the military blockade itself.
